newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro bourses score records, gold slides.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro bourses score records, gold slides.

text.p: Major European bourses hit record levels on Wednesday, after U.S. central bank head Alan Greenspan soothed investors' worst fears for now, before closing below their highest levels for the day.

The London and Paris stock markets rebounded to scale new peaks after Greenspan, who has spooked investors on various occasions with warning comments, again denied he was trying to talk Wall Street down.
He said current share price levels could be justified if earnings forecasts were right.
German shares rose further in after-hours electronic trading to add to a record close in earlier floor trade, aided by a steady dollar, good news for exporters.

"There are some decent volumes there and the greenback is helping, especially with the exporters. The slogan at the moment seems to be -- enjoy it and let the cash roll in," said Josh Waiblinger of equity sales at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
Wall Street also took heart from Greenspan's comments, with the Dow Jones industrial average gaining more than half a percent in morning trading in New York.

But the chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve, who sent stocks tumbling a week ago with a warning that Wall Street's rise had "raised questions of sustainability", was due to give yet another speech later on Wednesday -- encouraging caution.
Greenspan was set to give the second leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins Congressional testimony at 1900 GMT.
Gold slid to end London trading below $353, down around $7 on the day, on news of Swiss plans to sell gold from reserves to finance a fund for Holocaust victims and others.
Bullion analysts said the amount involved was unlikely to be large compared with overall market turnover but the news added to the pressure on gold.
"The amount is not huge by any means but it is indicative of central bank sentiment towards the market," one dealer said.
Concern that central banks would sell gold to help meet the economic criteria for joining European economic and monetary union had dented the gold price in past months.

On currency markets, meanwhile, the dollar traded below a new 34-month peak against the German currency of 1.7169 marks, hit in Asian business, and lost some ground against a firm Japanese yen at around 121.55 yen.
Currrency traders were now looking ahead to key jobs data later this week -- U.S. February non-farm payrolls data on Friday and German February unemployment numbers on Thursday.
"Ahead of tomorrow's numbers a bit of caution is required, so the mark's remaining pretty soft, though not ground-breakingly so," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered.
The dollar was boosted by a bigger than expected fall in German January output, down 1.7 percent, but the mark drew support from yet more speculation on delays in European monetary union.

Meanwhile, analysts said the yen gained from comments by Japanese chief cabinet secretary Seiroku Kajiyama that Tokyo should mull how to deal with the impact of low interest rates on incomes -- making the market more nervous about how long Japanese rates could remain low.
It was also helped by data showing Japan's trade surplus rose 53.3 percent year-on-year in the first 20 days of February.
The London stock market, Europe's busiest, had opened lower after a 66-point fall in the Dow Jones industrial average overnight and some disappointing corporate results.
Greenspan's reassuring comments later helped it climb into previously uncharted territory although weaker bond prices then brought it down from its highs.
"At these high levels the market seems to be struggling to make headway," said one senior trader, "but there are few sellers out there and when buyers come in it forces prices up."

British Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George held their monthly monetary meeting on Wednesday but, as expected this close to an election due by May, the central bank left official interest rates unchanged.

French shares also recovered from early losses to hit a record close but were below an earlier historic high scored after a rally underpinned by dollar strength and the rise on Wall Street, dealers said.
CURRENCIES AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was quoted around 1.7128 marks and 121.56 yen, compared with 1.7118 and 121.94 late on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index ended up 2.4 points or 0.06 percent at a record close of 4,360.1 after earlier hitting an all-time peak of 4,367.3.
PARIS - The CAC-40 gained 14.50 points, 0.55 percent, to a record 2,666.19 close after an earlier all-time high 2,676.55.

FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index ended floor trade up 44.33 at a record close of 3,364.99, near an all-time high during the session of 3,365.03. The IBIS DAX ended later computerised trading at 3,375.45, up 30.36 points or 0.91 percent but off an earlier peak of 3,392.13.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold weakened to end at $352.65 an ounce after an afternoon fix of $354.50 versus the previous London close of $359.80. Silver slipped six cents to $5.19.
